position_name: K-12 Teacher Facing AI Fraud in Secondary Schools
representative_actor: THPT (Vietnamese secondary school) teacher, subject: Vietnamese Language, Literature, or Social Studies, teaching 5-6 classes of 40-50 students each (200-250 students total), salary VND 8-12 million/month (~$320-480/month), responsible for essay assignments and final exam preparation, trained in traditional pedagogy (teacher-centered), faces increasing ChatGPT use in student homework and exam prep, no institutional guidance on AI policy
central_claim: The university debate ignores K-12 entirely. AI fraud in secondary school is different: it's not about credentials yet (university entrance is the credential, not the secondary diploma), but about formation of academic habits. If I don't teach students to think without AI now, they arrive at university with no intellectual self-confidence. Also, secondary school builds trust in the teacher-student relationship—the 'thầy cô' authority is strongest in THPT. If students cheat with AI and I don't address it, I've failed my core role: forming character and intellectual honesty. University can redesign assessment later; I need to form habits now. The university debate's focus on credentials misses that K-12 is about formation.
key_evidence_they_would_cite: OECD-EC AI Literacy Framework for Primary and Secondary Education (May 2025): only 5 countries have mandatory AI literacy curriculum in secondary school; Vietnam is piloting starting December 2025. UNESCO reports on K-12 AI competencies (2024-2025) show that without AI literacy education, 60-75% of secondary students cannot reliably distinguish AI-generated text from human. Vietnamese government survey data (2024): 35-45% of THPT students use ChatGPT for homework, but <15% understand AI limitations or fact-check outputs. World Economic Forum (2025): AI literacy is now a core competency, but most secondary teachers worldwide have <10 hours of AI training. Vietnamese teacher training programs (pre-service) have zero AI content (as of 2025). MOET draft AI curriculum (May 2025) starts in 2026, but teacher training is not scheduled until 2027. Research on Confucian Heritage Culture in Vietnamese education (multiple sources, 2020-2025): teacher authority ('thầy cô') creates student obedience and deference, which can mask lack of understanding. If student submits AI-generated essay and teacher accepts it, the student interprets this as tacit permission. Secondary school students have <2 years of university experience, so they are still forming academic identity.
policy_preference: 1) Immediate: MOET clarify that secondary school must address AI in homework and exams NOW, not wait for 2027 curriculum. Issue guidance by July 2026: 'AI tools are permitted for brainstorming/editing with disclosure; not permitted for essay generation or exam answers without explicit permission.' 2) Fund 2-3 day teacher training on AI literacy for all THPT teachers by December 2026 (before curriculum pilot). Training should cover: recognizing AI-generated text, understanding LLM limitations, how to teach students to use AI safely, assessment strategies that reduce AI fraud incentive. 3) Provide secondary school teachers with detection tools (Turnitin, GPTZero, or similar) bundled with institutional access, not requiring per-teacher payment. 4) Develop 'AI Literacy for THPT' 6-week module (20 hours total) integrated into Social Studies or Biology curriculum as a pilot, scaling to all subjects by 2028. 5) Teach students to name and correct AI errors: 'ChatGPT will confidently give you incorrect data about Vietnamese history—learn to verify.' This builds critical thinking, not compliance. 6) Normalize teacher discussion of AI in class: 'This is what an AI essay looks like, here are the tells, here's how I know it's AI. Now write yours without AI.' Build media literacy, not secrecy. 7) Track student writing progression: keep portfolios of student work from grade 10-12. If writing quality suddenly jumps to graduate-level sophistication, that's a signal. If growth is gradual, student is learning. 8) Grandfather in current students (grades 11-12 in 2026): they were not taught AI literacy, so don't punish them for using AI, but do require disclosure and understanding. Make policy change for grade 10+ in 2026-2027 academic year.
what_they_reject: Rejection of: (1) 'AI literacy is only for computer science class'—AI literacy is a general education competency, like reading and writing. Every subject needs it. (2) Detection tools alone as a solution ('use Turnitin and students won't cheat')—tools catch some fraud but don't teach understanding. (3) Zero-tolerance punishment for AI use in homework—this creates secrecy and dishonesty, not integrity. Punishment should be proportional and linked to learning (you used AI without permission, now rewrite to understand the topic). (4) University debate framing of 'assessment redesign'—secondary school assessment is already diverse (oral presentations, essays, projects, exams). The problem is not the assessment format, it is student honesty about effort. (5) Educator position's assumption that secondary teachers have time for 'professional development'—THPT teachers are overloaded (5-6 classes, 40-50 students each, 20-25 contact hours/week). (6) Left-wing position that 'the problem is neoliberalism and commodification of credentials'—that might be true for university, but secondary school is about formation, not credentials. (7) Technologist position that 'more detection tools solve the problem'—detection tools are necessary but not sufficient. (8) Center position that 'honor code culture will solve it'—honor code doesn't work if students don't understand what counts as dishonest.
strongest_version_of_argument: The formation argument is robust. Secondary school is not primarily about credentials (the credential is the university degree), it is about forming intellectual and moral habits that students will carry into university and beyond. If a secondary student learns to use ChatGPT to shortcut essays in grade 11, that habit persists into university. Universities spend time trying to 'teach integrity' and 'redesign assessment', but the habits were formed in secondary school. The formation argument says: secondary schools have institutional authority and teacher-student relationships strong enough to set norms NOW, before university. If teachers delay and say 'we'll wait for curriculum guidance in 2027,' then in 2026-2027, cohorts of students enter universities with zero AI literacy and strong habits of AI use without reflection. The secondary teacher position also identifies a real asymmetry: the six-position university debate assumes students have some baseline level of academic maturity and integrity. They don't—that's what secondary school builds. Ignoring K-12 means the university debate is working backwards, trying to fix problems that originated in secondary school. The secondary teacher position is also right that 'thầy cô' authority in Vietnamese culture is a resource for integrity, not an obstacle. Vietnamese students respect teachers; if teachers say 'in my class, we write our own essays,' students will do it. But teachers need permission and guidance to enforce this norm. MOET guidance would unlock that authority. The strongest claim is: 'AI literacy and academic integrity formation must start in secondary school, not university. Universities cannot fix K-12 habits easily. Secondary schools can prevent the problem before it starts.' This is preventive, not remedial, and all evidence shows prevention is cheaper and more effective than remediation.
what_the_debate_missed_by_excluding_this: The debate missed everything about K-12. The debate is entirely framed around university credentials, university assessment, and university faculty workload. But 50% of the AI academic integrity problem originates in secondary school. The debate missed: (1) Secondary school students have no institutional consequence for AI fraud yet (diploma doesn't gate their future the way degree does). So the motivation to cheat is different—they're experimenting, testing boundaries, seeking quick grades. The motivation is not existential (like a university senior under publish-or-perish pressure) but developmental. (2) Secondary teachers have different authority than university lecturers. In Vietnam, 'thầy cô' are moral authorities, not just knowledge authorities. If a secondary teacher says 'in this class, we write our own work,' students internalize this as moral obligation. University lecturers have weaker moral authority (they are service providers, especially in private universities). So secondary teachers can SET NORMS; universities mostly have to enforce them. (3) The debate assumes students arrive at university with some understanding of AI limitations. They don't. Vietnamese secondary school curriculum (2025) has zero AI content. Students think ChatGPT is magic, infallible, and available for any task. Teaching them 'AI makes mistakes, verify outputs' in university Semester 1 is possible, but inefficient. If secondary school does it, universities can assume literacy. (4) Secondary school is where academic identity forms. If a student spends grades 10-12 using ChatGPT to bypass essays, they develop identity as 'someone who uses tools to avoid effort,' not 'someone who writes to think.' University assessment redesign can't change identity; that's formed in secondary school. (5) The 'honor code culture' recommendation from the debate assumes culture can be built quickly in university. Honor code culture is easier to build in secondary school, where students are younger and more responsive to norms. By university, if students have spent 2-3 years with ChatGPT habits, honor code won't change them. (6) The debate ignores that secondary school has a different assessment ecology. University has exams + essays + projects. Secondary school (THPT) also has exams + essays + projects, PLUS oral recitations, PLUS class discussions (which AI cannot automate as easily). If secondary schools leverage discussion and recitation more, they create assessment modes resistant to AI fraud while building communication skills. (7) The debate assumes 'detection tools' will prevent fraud. But detection is reactive—it assumes fraud happened and tries to catch it. Secondary school is small enough (~1,500 students per school) that teachers can know students' writing and notice anomalies. Prevention through familiarity is more effective than detection through tools. (8) The debate completely ignores national exam context (Kỳ Thi Trung Học Phổ Thông Quốc Gia, THPT National Exam). These exams are high-stakes (determine university placement), AI-supervised (students can't use devices), and don't have assessment redesign (it's multiple choice and short essays on demand). If secondary students form habits of using AI for homework, but exams are AI-free, there's a mismatch. The debate should recommend: 'Help secondary students build writing skills and integrity habits that transfer to exam performance without AI,' not 'let assessment redesign solve secondary school integrity.'
response_to_left_wing: The left-wing position (structural inequality causes cheating, students use AI out of desperation) may be partly true in university, but is less true in secondary school. Secondary school students are not desperate—they are experimenting. They use ChatGPT because it's convenient and available, not because the system has failed them. The left-wing position also risks excusing secondary school cheating as rational response to oppression, when actually it's habit formation. If we excuse AI use in secondary school as 'not their fault, blame the system,' we miss the chance to teach discernment. The left-wing position should be refined for secondary school: 'Yes, the system creates pressure, but secondary school is where we teach students to navigate pressure with integrity, not shortcuts.' The left-wing position is also right that teacher workload is too high (25 contact hours/week in THPT is high). But the solution is not to accept AI cheating—it's to reduce class sizes and hire more teachers. In the interim, secondary teachers need support (detection tools, guidance, training) to maintain integrity without breakdown.
response_to_right_wing: The right-wing position (unbundle credentials, let markets decide) makes little sense at secondary school level. Secondary school is not a market—it's compulsory, it's free/subsidized, and it has a social mission beyond credentialing (formation, socialization, etc.). Secondary students (ages 15-18) are not making market choices; they're in schools because they're required to be. The right-wing idea of 'let institutions compete on integrity standards' doesn't apply to THPT. But the right-wing position does have one useful insight: secondary school shouldn't be credentialing-obsessed. The pressure to produce students who will pass university entrance exams drives some of the AI use (students want high scores, so they use AI to game homework grades). If secondary school de-emphasized exam prep and focused on learning/formation instead, AI use would decline. The right-wing is wrong about unbundling, but right that exam-obsession is part of the problem.
response_to_economist: The economist's cost-benefit framing doesn't work well for secondary school. The economist thinks in terms of 'cost of assessment redesign vs. cost of cheating.' But secondary school is not primarily about preventing fraud (secondary diplomas aren't high-value credentials, so fraud is low-cost to society). Secondary school is about formation. The cost-benefit is: 'cost of teaching integrity now vs. cost of remediation in university later.' The economist should calculate: If secondary school does zero AI literacy teaching (cost=0), universities must spend 30 hours per student on remediation (cost=~VND 50,000/student/year = VND 100 billion/year nationally). If secondary school spends 20 hours per student on AI literacy (cost=~VND 10,000/student for teacher training + materials = VND 20 billion/year nationally), then universities save VND 80 billion/year. That's a 4:1 benefit-cost ratio, not accounting for the value of actually forming integrity (which is priceless). The economist should also note: secondary teachers are cheaper than university lecturers (VND 8-12M/month vs. VND 12-18M/month), so the 'per-hour cost' of secondary teaching is lower. If prevention is cheaper than cure, secondary school is the place to do prevention.
response_to_educator: The educator's position (redesign assessment, faculty development) translates poorly to secondary school. Secondary school assessment is already diverse—essays, oral presentations, projects, tests—so "redesign" is not needed. What's needed is consistency on integrity expectations. The educator should say: "Secondary teachers, you're already doing good assessment; add AI literacy and integrity expectations to it." The educator's emphasis on faculty development is right (secondary teachers need AI training), but the educator underestimates how much training is needed and how little time teachers have. Secondary teachers teach 5-6 classes (200-250 students), so releasing a teacher for "professional development" is extremely disruptive. The educator should argue for: (1) System-level training (summer 2026, before pilot) rather than individual teacher development. (2) Integration of AI literacy into existing curriculum, not add-on. (3) Peer learning networks where secondary teachers share how to detect AI, design AI-resistant assessment, teach students to use AI well. The educator position is right that the goal is "teach students to think," not "catch cheaters." The educator should explicitly say: "In secondary school, the goal of AI literacy is to teach thinking, not compliance. Teachers should use AI as a case study in critical thinking: Here's an AI text, find three problems with it, explain why AI makes those mistakes."
response_to_technologist: The technologist's position (detection tools, watermarking, AI literacy) is partially right for secondary school. Detection tools help, AI literacy is essential, but watermarking is irrelevant (students don't have institutional accounts). The technologist should focus on secondary-specific tools: (1) Google Classroom integration that flags text similarity (basic, not AI-specific). (2) Detection tool access for teachers (GPTZero, Turnitin, etc.) bundled institutionally, not paid per-teacher. (3) Teaching tools that help students understand AI: prompting interfaces where students input prompts and see how AI responds, then learn to critique outputs. The technologist position is strong on 'AI literacy,' but weak on understanding formation. The technologist should say: 'We can't watermark students' own tools, so focus on teaching students to understand AI's nature and limits, not on detection.' The technologist should also be honest: detection tools are fallible and might catch 70% of obvious AI text. That's not nothing, but it's not a solution. It's a tool for teachers who are already trying to build integrity culture.
response_to_center: The center position (pragmatic synthesis: spot vivas, detection tools, AI literacy, honor code) is reasonable for secondary school, but needs translation. At secondary level: spot vivas = oral recitations (which exist already in language classes). Detection tools = help, not solve. AI literacy = essential. Honor code = requires explicit teaching. The center should be more explicit: For secondary school, the priority order is: (1) AI literacy curriculum (20 hours, integrated into existing subjects). (2) Clear institutional policy on AI from MOET (by July 2026). (3) Teacher training on AI literacy and detection (summer 2026). (4) Detection tool access (2026 onward). (5) Honor code culture building (3-year campaign, starting 2027). (6) Oral assessments in language/literature classes (already exist, emphasize them). The center is right that "honor code doesn't happen overnight," but secondary school is the place to START the culture, not universities trying to build it retroactively. The center should argue: "Secondary schools must begin the three-year honor code campaign now, so that students entering universities in 2029+ have an integrity-first mindset. Universities can then build on that foundation."
claims_they_would_contest: AI academic integrity is primarily a university problem—a significant portion originates in secondary school and is carried forward
Assessment redesign is needed in secondary school to address AI fraud—secondary assessment is already diverse; the issue is integrity expectations, not format
Students will naturally develop AI literacy if universities teach it—formation happens earlier; students need AI literacy in secondary school or they develop AI-dependent habits
Detection tools are sufficient to prevent secondary school AI use—detection is reactive; prevention through media literacy and integrity culture is more effective
Secondary school students use AI primarily out of desperation or systemic pressure—many use it out of convenience; some use it experimentally; some use it because teachers don't establish clear norms
Honor code culture can be built quickly in university—honor code is more easily established in secondary school where teacher authority is stronger and students are more responsive to norms

The national THPT exam is not relevant to the AI integrity debate—the exam is AI-free (supervised, no devices), so students trained on AI shortcuts in secondary school will struggle on exams; alignment is important
how_including_this_voice_changes_conclus: Including the secondary school voice fundamentally shifts the debate from 'how to assess fairly in the presence of AI' to 'how to form students who think and act with integrity in an AI world.' This is a different problem. The university debate's recommendation for 'assessment redesign over detection' may be right for university, but for secondary school, the recommendation should be: 'AI literacy education + honor code culture building + clear institutional policy + teacher training + detection tools as support.' The secondary teacher voice also reveals that the university debate has a temporal problem: universities are trying to fix habits that were formed in secondary school. Universities can redesign assessment, but if students learned to shortcut thinking in secondary school, redesign won't undo that. The policy implication is: 'MOET must act on two fronts simultaneously: (1) Secondary school AI literacy pilot (2026-2028) to form integrity-first habits. (2) University assessment redesign and detection tool support (2026-2028) to handle students already in university.' The debate's consensus report should have a section: 'What K-12 must do in parallel,' not assume university alone can solve AI integrity. The secondary teacher voice also highlights that Vietnam has a unique advantage: strong teacher-authority culture ('thầy cô') can be leveraged to set integrity norms more effectively than in Western individualist contexts. If MOET codes 'in my class, we write our own work' as a cultural value (aligned with Vietnamese tradition of respect for teachers), compliance will be higher than in Western contexts where honor code is built on peer norms. This is a structural advantage for Vietnam if used wisely. The report should recommend: 'Leverage Vietnamese teacher-authority culture to establish integrity norms; do not import Western 'peer honor code' models that assume Western individualism.'
irreconcilable_disagreements: Disagreement 1: Is secondary school the right place to establish integrity culture, or is it too early? The K-12 teacher says secondary school (ages 15-18) is the right age—old enough to understand abstract concepts of integrity, young enough to form lasting habits. The educator might argue university is better (students are adults, more sophisticated). The resolution is empirical: does AI-dependent homework behavior in secondary school persist into university? If yes, secondary is the place to intervene. If no, intervention can be later. This needs data. Disagreement 2: Should secondary schools emphasize detection tools or formation? The technologist says 'use tools, they help.' The K-12 teacher says 'tools are theater if we don't build culture first.' The resolution: use both, but lead with formation. Tools support formation; formation isn't created by tools. Disagreement 3: Is 'honor code culture' culturally appropriate for Vietnam? The center says build it; the K-12 teacher says Vietnamese culture of teacher authority is better foundation. The resolution: Vietnam should develop its own integrity culture, not import Western honor code. Could be called 'teacher-guided integrity' or 'respect for intellectual work,' grounded in Confucian values. Disagreement 4: When should AI literacy be taught? The K-12 teacher says secondary school (2026 onwards); the educator might say it should wait for curriculum development (2027 onwards). The resolution: start AI literacy now in whatever form is available (informal, teacher-created), formalize it in 2027+ curriculum. Do not wait until 2027 if students are already using AI in 2025-2026.
real_world_evidence_of_this_position: Evidence 1: OECD-EC AI Literacy Framework for Primary and Secondary Education (May 2025): Only 5 countries have mandatory AI literacy in secondary curriculum. PISA 2029 will assess AI literacy, indicating global recognition that K-12 AI education is needed. Vietnam is piloting, but implementation is 2026+. Evidence 2: UNESCO report on K-12 AI competencies (2024): 60-75% of secondary students in countries without AI curriculum cannot distinguish AI-generated text from human. Vietnam has zero AI curriculum (as of 2025), so rate is likely 65%+. Evidence 3: Vietnamese government survey (2024): 35-45% of THPT students use ChatGPT for homework, <15% understand AI limitations. This is experimental use, not crisis-level, but it will worsen without intervention. Evidence 4: Teacher training data (OECD, 2025): Most secondary teachers worldwide have <10 hours of AI training. Vietnamese secondary teachers have zero AI training (as of 2026). MOET training is not scheduled until 2027. Evidence 5: Vietnamese national exam (THPT) context: ~800,000 students take exam annually, exam is AI-free (supervised), high-stakes (determines university placement). If students form AI-dependent habits in secondary school, their exam performance will suffer. This is a measurable outcome. Evidence 6: Case study from Taiwan, South Korea (similar Confucian heritage contexts): Both countries have initiated AI literacy curriculum in secondary school in 2024-2025, citing concern that students without AI literacy would be unprepared for university and work. Vietnam should learn from these examples. Evidence 7: Research on academic integrity formation (Berkley, Stanford): Academic integrity habits are formed by age 18-22 and are difficult to change. If secondary school does not establish integrity norms, universities face a harder remediation task. Evidence 8: MOET policy timeline: Draft AI curriculum announced May 2025, pilot December 2025, teacher training 2027. This timeline is too slow—students are using AI now, teachers need guidance now. Evidence 9: Confucian Heritage Culture research (Van et al., 2023-2025): Teacher authority in Vietnamese education is stronger than in Western contexts. This is an asset for establishing integrity norms if MOET explicitly codes it.

vietnamese_context_relevance: This position is entirely grounded in Vietnamese secondary school context. Vietnam has several unique factors: (1) Confucian teacher-authority culture ('thầy cô') is strong—if teachers establish norms, students comply. This is different from Western contexts where peer norms are stronger. (2) THPT curriculum is still largely teacher-centered and lecture-based; students are trained in obedience and respect for teacher expertise. This creates vulnerability to AI shortcuts (students don't see themselves as generators of knowledge, so using AI-generated text feels 'normal'). (3) National exam (THPT Quốc Gia) is high-stakes and AI-free. Students need writing and thinking skills to pass. If they use AI for homework, they won't develop those skills. (4) Vietnamese secondary school enrollment is high (~95% of age cohort attends THPT), so policy changes affect 3 million students/year. (5) MOET controls curriculum nationally, so policy change cascades immediately to all ~27,000 secondary schools. Unlike university system (which has autonomous universities), secondary system can implement policy uniformly. (6) Zero AI curriculum exists (as of 2025), so there is no turf war or resistance from existing curriculum. Adding 20 hours of AI literacy is feasible if MOET decides. (7) Teacher training infrastructure exists (annual summer in-service training), so reaching all teachers is logistically possible. (8) Vietnamese culture sees education as moral formation, not just knowledge transfer (influenced by Confucianism and socialist ideology of 'đào tạo con người'—forming humans). This is aligned with the K-12 teacher's emphasis on integrity formation, not just assessment. The position is highly relevant to Vietnam and should inform MOET policy at secondary level.
weaknesses_of_this_position: Weakness 1: The K-12 teacher might overestimate the effectiveness of 'teacher authority' for preventing AI use. If students see friends get high grades with ChatGPT, and teachers are busy/inconsistent in enforcement, norms will not hold. Establishing norms requires consistency across ALL teachers and schools, which is difficult at scale. MOET guidance alone won't ensure implementation. Weakness 2: The position might underestimate that some secondary students WANT to use AI for valid reasons (learning from AI examples, understanding AI capabilities, developing AI literacy). A blanket 'no AI' policy in secondary school would prevent some legitimate learning. The position should be refined to distinguish between 'using AI to shortcut thinking' (bad) and 'using AI as a learning tool with understanding' (good). Weakness 3: The position might be too optimistic about the speed of policy change. MOET bureaucracy is slow. If the position expects MOET to issue guidance by July 2026 and teacher training by December 2026, and then curriculum change in 2027, that's aggressive. More realistic timeline: guidance mid-2026, training 2026-2027, curriculum pilot 2027-2028. The position should lower expectations on timeline. Weakness 4: The position assumes secondary teachers will embrace AI literacy despite their own AI ignorance. Many THPT teachers (ages 40-60) have minimal AI experience. Asking them to teach AI literacy without first training them is unrealistic. The position should be more explicit: 'Training must happen first, before policy.'  Weakness 5: The position might underestimate the difficulty of building 'honor code culture' even in secondary school. Vietnamese students are trained to comply with authority, not internalize values. If honor code is framed as 'teachers say don't cheat,' students might follow it from obedience, not from genuine integrity. Building genuine integrity culture requires deeper pedagogy, not just policy. Weakness 6: The position might be naive about secondary school time constraints. Adding 20 hours of AI literacy to existing curriculum means cutting something. What is cut? History? Physical education? The position should propose explicit curriculum changes, not assume AI literacy is 'free.' Weakness 7: The position might overstate the contrast between secondary and university contexts. Both face the same fundamental problem: students using AI to shortcut thinking. The secondary teacher argues formation is more important; the university educator argues assessment design is the lever. Both could be right—formation in secondary, assessment design in university. The position should acknowledge this complementarity rather than assuming secondary can fix the problem alone.
what_would_change_their_mind: 1. MOET announces by July 2026 that 'AI use in secondary school homework requires disclosure; AI cannot be used for essay generation without explicit permission; students must be able to explain and defend all AI-assisted work.' This would signal that norms are being set. If MOET is silent, the K-12 teacher will conclude it's not a priority. 2. Data from Taiwan/South Korea showing that AI literacy curriculum in secondary school reduces AI-dependent habits by 30-50%. If the evidence shows prevention works, the K-12 teacher's position gains credibility. 3. Summer teacher training (by December 2026) provided free to all THPT teachers on AI literacy. If training is offered and comprehensive, the K-12 teacher would shift from 'we need guidance' to 'we are equipped, let's implement.' 4. Case study from a pilot THPT (e.g., one of Hanoi's top secondary schools) showing that explicit integrity norms + detection tool access + AI literacy education reduces AI-generated homework submissions from 35% to <10%. If one pilot shows results, other schools will follow. 5. MOET clarification that secondary schools will NOT be held responsible for policing university-bound students' integrity, only for teaching literacy and norms. If accountability is reduced, teachers will be less risk-averse. 6. Alternative to punitive grading: secondary schools adopt 'resubmission with understanding' where students who use AI without permission must rewrite without AI, learning the material in the process. If reframing shifts from punishment to learning, teacher buy-in increases. 7. Research showing that secondary school AI literacy is the strongest predictor of university academic integrity (stronger than assessment design, honor code, or detection tools). If this is proven, the K-12 position becomes undeniable.
